options.text: A situation where two threads access shared data simultaneously, leading to unpredictable results.
A condition where a program runs slower due to multiple threads.
A scenario where threads are executed in a predetermined order.
A situation where a single thread executes a task without interruption.

questions.explanation: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access shared data at the same time, and the final outcome depends on the sequence of execution, which can lead to unpredictable results.

distractorRationale.b: This describes a performance issue, not a race condition.
distractorRationale.c: Race conditions involve unpredictable execution order, not predetermined.
distractorRationale.d: This describes atomic operations, not race conditions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for solving the critical section problem?

options.text: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
Deadlock prevention

questions.explanation: The critical section problem requires mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Deadlock prevention is important in concurrency but is not specifically a requirement for the critical section problem.

distractorRationale.a: Mutual exclusion is a key requirement for critical sections.
distractorRationale.b: Progress ensures that threads can enter the critical section when it is free.
distractorRationale.c: Bounded waiting prevents starvation of threads waiting to enter the critical section.

questions.stem: If a shared counter is incremented by two threads 1000 times each without synchronization, what is the minimum possible final value of the counter? Assume the initial value is 0.
questions.explanation: Without synchronization, both threads could read the same value and increment it, leading to lost updates. The minimum value occurs when all increments from one thread are lost, resulting in only 1000 successful increments.

questions.stem: Why is the increment operation `x++` not considered atomic?

options.text: It involves multiple steps: read, increment, and write.
It is executed in a single CPU cycle.
It does not require any synchronization.
It is always executed without interruption.

questions.explanation: The increment operation `x++` is not atomic because it consists of multiple steps: reading the current value, incrementing it, and writing it back. These steps can be interleaved with other operations, leading to race conditions.

distractorRationale.b: The operation is not executed in a single CPU cycle; it involves multiple steps.
distractorRationale.c: Synchronization is required to ensure atomicity, which `x++` lacks.
distractorRationale.d: The operation can be interrupted, leading to race conditions.

questions.stem: Explain the concept of mutual exclusion and why it is important in preventing race conditions.
markingGuide: Define mutual exclusion as allowing only one thread to execute in the critical section at a time.
Explain that mutual exclusion prevents race conditions by ensuring that shared resources are not accessed simultaneously by multiple threads.
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion is a fundamental concept in concurrency control, ensuring that only one thread can access the critical section at any given time. This prevents race conditions by avoiding simultaneous access to shared resources, which can lead to inconsistent states and unpredictable results.

questions.stem: Which condition ensures that a thread will eventually enter the critical section after requesting access?

options.text: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
Deadlock prevention

questions.explanation: Bounded waiting ensures that there is a limit on the number of times other threads can enter the critical section after a thread has requested access, preventing starvation and ensuring eventual entry.

distractorRationale.a: Mutual exclusion ensures only one thread accesses the critical section at a time.
distractorRationale.b: Progress ensures that if no thread is in the critical section, one can enter.
distractorRationale.d: Deadlock prevention is not directly related to ensuring eventual entry.

questions.explanation: The maximum value occurs when all increments are successful without any lost updates. With three threads incrementing 500 times each, the maximum possible final value is 1500.

questions.stem: Discuss the importance of the progress condition in the critical section problem.
markingGuide: Define the progress condition as ensuring that if no thread is in the critical section, one of the waiting threads can enter.
Explain that progress prevents unnecessary delays and ensures efficient use of resources.
questions.explanation: The progress condition is crucial in ensuring that the system does not waste time when the critical section is free. It guarantees that if no thread is currently executing in the critical section, one of the waiting threads will be allowed to enter, thus preventing unnecessary delays and improving system efficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the bounded waiting condition?

options.text: A limit on the number of threads that can enter the critical section simultaneously.
A limit on the number of times other threads can enter the critical section after a thread has requested access.
A limit on the time a thread can spend in the critical section.
A limit on the number of threads that can request access to the critical section.

questions.explanation: Bounded waiting ensures that there is a limit on how many times other threads can enter the critical section after a thread has requested access, preventing starvation and ensuring fairness.

distractorRationale.a: This describes mutual exclusion, not bounded waiting.
distractorRationale.c: This describes a time limit, not bounded waiting.
distractorRationale.d: This does not relate to the bounded waiting condition.

questions.stem: Why is it important to ensure that operations on shared data are atomic in concurrent programming?
markingGuide: Define atomic operations as those that complete in a single step relative to other threads.
Explain that atomic operations prevent race conditions by ensuring that shared data is not accessed simultaneously by multiple threads.
questions.explanation: Atomic operations are crucial in concurrent programming because they ensure that operations on shared data are completed without interruption. This prevents race conditions by ensuring that no other thread can access the data until the operation is complete, maintaining data consistency and integrity.
